segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is also a deacon of the assembly in Cenchreae,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the holy ones and stand by her in whatever matter she may need you; for she herself has been a patron of many, and of me myself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my co-workers in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who risked their own necks for my life; not only I but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles give thanks to them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet also the assembly that meets in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Asia for Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Mary, who has worked very hard for you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kin and my fellow prisoners, who are outstanding among the apostles and who were in Christ before I was.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Urbanus, our co-worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Apelles, proven in Christ. Greet those from the household of Aristobulus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those from the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who work hard in the Lord. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked very hard in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is mine as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the holy ones with them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the assemblies of Christ greet you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urge you, brothers and sisters, to watch out for those who cause divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you learned; turn away from them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For such people are slaves not to our Lord Christ but to their own belly, and by smooth talk and fine-sounding words they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For word of your obedience has reached everyone, so I rejoice over you; but I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Timothy, my co-worker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason and Sosipater, my kin.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, as does our brother Quartus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

notes.note: The Greek word ordinarily means someone who serves or carries out a task for another, and elsewhere in this translation it is 'servant'. Here it is tied to a particular assembly ('a deacon of the assembly in Cenchreae'), which suggests a recognised role, so 'deacon' is used. This is disputed: many translations have 'servant', and how formal such roles were at this early date is uncertain. The word is the same form used for men; 'deaconess' reflects a later, separate office.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution, neither of which existed. This translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs.

The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. 'Saints', kept by many translations, now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Others render it 'God's people'.

The word is the feminine of a term for a patron, protector or presiding figure: someone of means and standing who used them on behalf of others. Older translations have 'helper', which undersells it; several recent ones have 'benefactor' or 'patron'. It echoes the verb just translated 'stand by': the Romans are to stand by her because she has stood up for many.

The Greek word is the ordinary one for 'nations' or 'peoples'; in Jewish usage the plural meant the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it 'Gentiles' in that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant. It is one Greek word throughout.

Asia here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, whose chief city was Ephesus, not the continent. 'Firstfruits' is a harvest image from Israel's offerings: Epaenetus was the first convert there, with the rest of the harvest to follow.

The Greek form could in theory belong to a man's name, 'Junias', and many twentieth-century translations printed it that way. But no such male name has been found in ancient sources, whereas Junia was a common Latin woman's name, and early Christian commentators took her to be a woman. Most scholars now read Junia, probably the wife or sister of Andronicus.

The phrase can also be read 'well known to the apostles', which would leave Andronicus and Junia outside that group; some recent translations take it so. The majority of scholars, and the early Greek-speaking interpreters, read it as counting them among the apostles. 'Apostles' would then have its wider sense of commissioned emissaries, not the Twelve.

The word means a relative, but Paul uses it in Romans 9:3 for his fellow Jews as a whole. Since six people in this chapter are so described (also verses 11 and 21), most scholars think he means fellow Jews, not members of his family. 'Kin' leaves both readings open.

notes.phrase: those from the household of Aristobulus
notes.traditional: those of the household of Aristobulus
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'those from among Aristobulus's people'. A wealthy household included slaves and freed slaves, and it is some of these who are greeted, not Aristobulus himself, who may not have been a believer or even still alive. The same applies to Narcissus in the next verse. Attempts to identify the two men with known figures in Rome are plausible but unproven.

The verb belongs to the word group for slavery and means to be someone's slave, which is stronger than 'serve'. This translation keeps slave language distinct from the separate word group for service, the one behind 'deacon' in verse 1.

Letters were normally dictated to a secretary, and here the secretary adds his own greeting in the first person. 'In the Lord' may go with 'greet you', as translated, or with 'wrote down this letter'.

notes.phrase: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.
notes.note: This verse is absent from the earliest manuscripts and omitted by many modern editions and translations, which regard it as a repetition of the blessing in verse 20. The Greek edition translated here includes it, and does not include the doxology that most Bibles print as verses 25–27. That doxology appears at different places in different manuscripts (here, after 14:23, or after 15:33), and its originality is disputed.

candidates.rendering: brothers and sisters (plural, of the community); brother (singular)
candidates.reason: The plural addresses mixed communities throughout the letters and translations split between 'brothers', 'brethren' and 'brothers and sisters'; one policy is needed.
It can mean family relative or fellow Jew (Romans 9:3; 16:7, 11, 21; Luke), and the English should not vary arbitrarily between 'relatives', 'kinsmen' and 'fellow Jews'.
It recurs across the Gospels and letters with renderings ranging from 'offence' and 'obstacle' to 'stumbling block' and 'trap', and the cognate verb needs a matching decision.
The register separates δοῦλος from διάκονος, and the cognate verb needs the same decision so that 'serve' is not shared between the two word groups.
It is Paul's regular term for his associates across several letters, and translations vary between 'fellow worker', 'co-worker' and 'helper'.
